questions.title: Total body water in a 70 kg adult
questions.question: The total water content in the body equals ………… in a person 70 kg

explanations.A: Correct. Total body water (TBW) is about 60% of body weight in a normal adult male. For a 70 kg reference adult, 60% of 70 kg is 42 L -- the standard worked figure this whole compartment scheme is built from, since the ICF, ECF, interstitial and plasma volumes are all fractions of this same 42 L.
explanations.B: Incorrect. 28 L is the intracellular fluid (ICF) volume for this same 70 kg adult (two-thirds of TBW), not the total body water figure this question asks for.
explanations.C: Incorrect. 14 L is the extracellular fluid (ECF) volume (one-third of TBW), a subcompartment of total body water, not the total itself.
explanations.D: Incorrect. 10 L is the interstitial fluid volume, a subcompartment within the ECF -- far short of the 42 L total body water figure.

questions.subject: fnd
questions.learning_objective: State total body water for a 70 kg reference adult as 42 L.

questions.title: Intracellular fluid volume in a 70 kg adult
questions.question: The total water content in the intracellular fluid equals ………. in a person 70 kg

explanations.A: Incorrect. 42 L is total body water for this same 70 kg adult, the sum of ICF and ECF, not the ICF figure alone.
explanations.B: Correct. The intracellular fluid (ICF) compartment holds two-thirds of total body water. For a 70 kg adult with 42 L total body water, two-thirds is 28 L -- the largest single fluid compartment in the body, since every cell's own cytoplasm contributes to it.
explanations.C: Incorrect. 14 L is the extracellular fluid (ECF) volume, the other one-third of total body water, not the ICF figure.
explanations.D: Incorrect. 10 L is the interstitial fluid volume, a subcompartment of the ECF -- a different, smaller compartment than the ICF this question asks about.

questions.subject: fnd
questions.learning_objective: State intracellular fluid volume for a 70 kg reference adult as 28 L.

questions.title: Extracellular fluid volume in a 70 kg adult
questions.question: The total water content in the extracellular fluid equals …………… in a person 70 kg

explanations.A: Incorrect. 42 L is total body water for this same 70 kg adult, the sum of ECF and ICF together, not the ECF figure alone.
explanations.B: Incorrect. 28 L is the intracellular fluid (ICF) volume, the other, larger two-thirds of total body water, not the ECF figure.
explanations.C: Correct. The extracellular fluid (ECF) compartment holds one-third of total body water. For a 70 kg adult with 42 L total body water, one-third is 14 L, split further into plasma (about 3 L) and interstitial fluid (about 10 L).
explanations.D: Incorrect. 10 L is only the interstitial fluid subcompartment within the ECF, not the ECF total, which also includes plasma.

questions.subject: fnd
questions.learning_objective: State extracellular fluid volume for a 70 kg reference adult as 14 L.

questions.title: Interstitial fluid volume in a 70 kg adult
questions.question: The total water content in the interstitial spaces equals in a person 70 kg

explanations.A: Incorrect. 42 L is total body water for this same 70 kg adult, far larger than the interstitial fluid subcompartment this question asks about.
explanations.B: Incorrect. 28 L is the intracellular fluid (ICF) volume, an entirely different (and much larger) compartment than the interstitial fluid.
explanations.C: Incorrect. 14 L is the full extracellular fluid (ECF) volume, which includes both interstitial fluid and plasma together, not the interstitial figure alone.
explanations.D: Correct. Interstitial fluid, the fluid bathing cells outside the capillary wall, is about 10 L for a 70 kg adult. It is the larger of the ECF's two subcompartments, the remainder once the directly-measured plasma volume (about 3 L) is subtracted from the 14 L ECF total. Unlike plasma, interstitial fluid volume is never measured directly, only calculated this way.

questions.subject: fnd
questions.learning_objective: State interstitial fluid volume for a 70 kg reference adult as about 10 L, as the ECF remainder after plasma.

questions.title: Plasma volume in a 70 kg adult
questions.question: The total water content in the plasma equals in a person 70 kg

explanations.A: Incorrect. 42 L is total body water for this same 70 kg adult, far larger than the plasma subcompartment this question asks about.
explanations.B: Incorrect. 28 L is the intracellular fluid (ICF) volume, an entirely different (and much larger) compartment than plasma.
explanations.C: Incorrect. 14 L is the full extracellular fluid (ECF) volume, which includes both plasma and interstitial fluid together, not plasma alone.
explanations.D: Incorrect. 10 L is the interstitial fluid volume, the other ECF subcompartment -- larger than, and separate from, plasma.
explanations.E: Correct. Plasma, the fluid inside blood vessels, is about 3 L for a 70 kg adult. It is the smaller of the ECF's two subcompartments, and the only body fluid compartment measured directly, by tracer dilution. Every other compartment's volume in this scheme is calculated as a fraction of total body water or as a remainder, not measured this directly.

questions.subject: fnd
questions.learning_objective: State plasma volume for a 70 kg reference adult as about 3 L, the only directly-measured compartment.

questions.title: Transcellular fluid volume in a 70 kg adult
questions.question: The total water content in the transcellular fluid in a person 70 kg

explanations.A: Incorrect. 14 L is the full extracellular fluid (ECF) volume, vastly larger than the small, specialised transcellular compartment this question asks about.
explanations.B: Incorrect. 10 L is the interstitial fluid volume, a much larger ECF subcompartment than transcellular fluid.
explanations.C: Incorrect. 3 L is the plasma volume, itself far larger than the transcellular compartment despite plasma being the smallest of the main ECF subdivisions.
explanations.D: Correct. Transcellular fluid -- CSF, synovial fluid, intraocular fluid, digestive secretions and similar specialised fluids not in free equilibrium with plasma or interstitial fluid -- is small, about 0.5 L for a 70 kg adult. It is often left out of the basic ICF/ECF breakdown entirely because of its small size and separate handling. Each of its individual sub-sites (CSF, synovial fluid, and the rest) is even smaller still.

questions.subject: fnd
questions.learning_objective: State transcellular fluid volume for a 70 kg reference adult as about 0.5 L.

questions.title: Protein concentration: plasma vs interstitial fluid
questions.question: Which of the following is in higher concentration in plasma than interstitial space:

explanations.A: Incorrect. Sodium is the dominant ECF cation in both plasma and interstitial fluid at nearly identical concentration -- the capillary wall is freely permeable to small ions, so sodium does not build up preferentially on either side.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Potassium, like sodium, crosses the capillary wall freely and sits at nearly the same low concentration in plasma and interstitial fluid; it is not the substance this question isolates.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Glucose also crosses the capillary wall freely and is present at essentially the same concentration in plasma and interstitial fluid, not preferentially retained in plasma.
explanations.D: Correct. Plasma proteins (chiefly albumin) are too large to cross the capillary wall freely, so plasma carries a much higher protein concentration than interstitial fluid, even though the two fluids are otherwise nearly identical extracellular fluid. This protein difference is exactly what generates the plasma colloidal osmotic pressure.

questions.subject: fnd
questions.learning_objective: Identify plasma proteins as the substance present at a higher concentration in plasma than in interstitial fluid.

questions.title: Barrier between ICF and ECF
questions.question: ICF and ECF are separated by:

explanations.A: Correct. The cell membrane (plasma membrane) is the barrier between the intracellular fluid (ICF) inside a cell and the extracellular fluid (ECF) surrounding it. This is the boundary at the level of a single cell, distinct from the capillary wall one level up in the ECF. It is selectively permeable, restricting most solutes and ions unless a specific channel or carrier lets them cross.
explanations.B: Incorrect. The capillary wall is a different, more permeable barrier one level up within the ECF itself, separating plasma from interstitial fluid, not ICF from ECF.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Tight junctions are a specialised feature of certain epithelia (e.g. the blood-brain barrier), not the general barrier separating ICF from ECF across the body.
explanations.D: Incorrect. ICF and ECF are physically separated by the cell membrane; they are not a single, undivided compartment.

questions.subject: fnd
questions.learning_objective: Identify the cell membrane as the barrier separating ICF from ECF.

questions.title: Barrier between plasma and interstitial fluid
questions.question: Plasma and interstitial fluid are separated by:

explanations.A: Incorrect. The cell membrane is the barrier between ICF and ECF at the level of a single cell, not the barrier this question asks about, which is within the ECF itself.
explanations.B: Correct. The capillary wall (vessel endothelium) is the barrier between plasma, inside blood vessels, and interstitial fluid, outside them around the cells. It is freely permeable to water and small solutes, but it restricts large plasma proteins. That protein restriction is exactly what allows plasma to carry a higher protein concentration than interstitial fluid, driving Starling's reabsorbing force.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Tight junctions are a specialised epithelial feature (e.g. the blood-brain barrier), not the general barrier separating plasma from interstitial fluid.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Plasma and interstitial fluid are physically separated by the capillary wall; they are not a single, undivided compartment.

questions.subject: fnd
questions.learning_objective: Identify the capillary wall as the barrier separating plasma from interstitial fluid.

questions.title: Reabsorbing force from interstitial fluid to plasma
questions.question: The reabsorbing force of fluids from interstitial fluid to the plasma is:

explanations.A: Incorrect. Capillary hydrostatic pressure pushes fluid out of the capillary into the interstitial space -- the filtering force, the opposite direction from the reabsorbing force this question asks about.
explanations.B: Correct. Plasma colloidal osmotic pressure (oncotic pressure), generated by plasma's higher protein concentration relative to interstitial fluid, pulls water back into the capillary from the interstitial space. It is the reabsorbing force in Starling's balance across the capillary wall. It opposes capillary hydrostatic pressure, which pushes fluid the opposite way, out of the capillary.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Interstitial fluid hydrostatic pressure, where present, also opposes filtration out of the capillary, but it is a hydrostatic, not the colloidal osmotic, force, and is not the reabsorbing force named here.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Interstitial fluid colloidal osmotic pressure would pull fluid out of the capillary (favouring filtration, not reabsorption), since interstitial fluid has a lower, not higher, protein concentration than plasma.

questions.subject: fnd
questions.learning_objective: Identify plasma colloidal osmotic pressure as the force reabsorbing fluid from interstitial space into the capillary.

questions.title: Cause of non-pitting oedema
questions.question: Which of the following causes non-pitting oedema:

explanations.A: Incorrect. Heart failure raises capillary hydrostatic pressure, producing ordinary pitting oedema (free interstitial fluid that can be displaced), not non-pitting oedema.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Venous obstruction by thrombosis also raises hydrostatic pressure upstream of the block, producing pitting, not non-pitting, oedema.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Liver failure lowers plasma colloidal osmotic pressure (via reduced albumin synthesis), producing pitting oedema, the same mechanism family as heart failure and venous obstruction, not the non-pitting pattern.
explanations.D: Correct. Lymphatic obstruction prevents the lymphatics from draining protein-rich interstitial fluid back to the circulation. That fluid accumulates and organises with the tissue rather than flowing freely. The result is oedema that is characteristically non-pitting, unlike the hydrostatic- or oncotic-pressure-driven causes above.

questions.subject: fnd
questions.learning_objective: Identify lymphatic obstruction as the cause of non-pitting oedema, distinguishing it from hydrostatic/oncotic causes of pitting oedema.

questions.title: Outermost covering of the axon
questions.question: Which of the following is the outermost layer that covers the axon of the nerve cell:

explanations.A: Incorrect. The cell membrane (axolemma) is the axon's own innermost membrane, not its outermost covering.
explanations.B: Incorrect. The myelin sheath, where present, lies internal to the neurilemmal sheath -- the next layer out from the axolemma, but not the outermost layer.
explanations.C: Correct. The neurilemmal sheath (sheath of Schwann) -- the Schwann cell's own cytoplasm and nucleus -- is the outermost covering of a peripheral axon. It surrounds both myelinated and unmyelinated fibres alike. It is also what makes peripheral nerve regeneration possible after injury, guiding a regrowing axon back toward its target.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Neurofibrils are intracellular cytoskeletal structures within the axon itself, not an outer covering layer at all.

questions.subject: neuro
questions.learning_objective: Identify the neurilemmal sheath as the outermost covering of a peripheral axon.

questions.title: Ionic basis of depolarization
questions.question: During the depolarization phase of the nerve action potential:

options.A: there is an increased influx of both K+ and Cl- ions
options.B: the membrane becomes more permeable to K+ than Na+ ions
options.C: there is an increased influx of Na+ ions
options.D: Na+ channels are blocked by Ca++ ions

explanations.A: Incorrect. Depolarization is driven by Na+ influx, not by an increased influx of K+ (which normally moves out, not in) and Cl- together -- neither the ion nor the direction named here matches the actual mechanism.
explanations.B: Incorrect. This reverses the depolarization-phase permeability change: during depolarization, the membrane becomes more permeable to Na+ than K+ (the opposite of the resting state), not more permeable to K+ than Na+.
explanations.C: Correct. Depolarization is caused by voltage-gated Na+ channels opening, letting Na+ move down its steep electrochemical gradient into the cell. This Na+ influx drives the membrane potential toward the sodium equilibrium potential. It produces the rising phase of the action potential, the fastest of the four ion-channel-linked mechanisms.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Na+ channels are not blocked by Ca++ during depolarization; on the contrary, they are actively opening to let Na+ influx happen, which is exactly what depolarization consists of.

questions.subject: neuro
questions.learning_objective: State that depolarization of the nerve action potential is caused by increased sodium influx.

questions.title: Resting membrane permeability: K+ vs Na+
questions.question: Resting nerve cell membrane is more permeable to :

options.A: K+ ions than to Na+ ions
options.B: organic anions than to Cl-- ions
options.C: glucose molecules than to oxygen molecules
options.D: calcium ions than to K + ions

explanations.A: Correct. At rest, the nerve membrane is far more permeable to potassium (K+), through leak channels, than it is to sodium (Na+). This permeability ratio is why the resting membrane potential sits close to the potassium equilibrium potential, well negative to threshold. It also means small K+ leaks matter far more to the resting value than equally-sized Na+ leaks do.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Organic anions are largely confined intracellularly and do not cross the resting membrane freely at all; this comparison does not describe the resting membrane's actual dominant permeability, which is the K+-over-Na+ ratio.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Oxygen, a small lipid-soluble gas, diffuses across the membrane extremely readily, more readily than glucose (which needs a facilitated transporter) -- this option reverses the expected relative permeability and is not the fact this question tests regardless.
explanations.D: Incorrect. The resting membrane's permeability to calcium is very low, not higher than to potassium; the defining resting-permeability relationship taught here is specifically K+ over Na+.

questions.subject: neuro
questions.learning_objective: State that the resting nerve membrane is more permeable to K+ than to Na+.

questions.title: Which permeability rise gives the greatest depolarization
questions.question: The membrane potential will depolarize by the greatest amount if the membrane permeability increases for:

explanations.A: Incorrect. Increased potassium permeability moves the membrane potential toward the (negative) potassium equilibrium potential, hyperpolarizing rather than depolarizing the membrane -- the opposite direction from what this question asks about.
explanations.B: Correct. Depolarization is caused by rising sodium permeability, and its size tracks the size of that rise. Increasing Na+ permeability alone drives the membrane potential furthest toward the positive sodium equilibrium potential. Among these four options, that gives the greatest depolarization.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Raising both sodium and potassium permeability together partly cancels the depolarizing effect of Na+ alone, since the simultaneous K+ permeability rise pulls the potential back toward rest -- a smaller net depolarization than sodium alone produces.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Increased chloride permeability moves the membrane potential toward the (negative) chloride equilibrium potential, which stabilises or hyperpolarizes the membrane rather than depolarizing it.

questions.subject: neuro
questions.learning_objective: Identify a rise in sodium permeability alone as producing the greatest depolarization among the listed permeability changes.

questions.title: RMP shift toward threshold and excitability
questions.question: Concerning the nerve fiber membrane at rest, the following is true:

options.A: the concentration gradient for K+ is such that it tends to move into fiber
options.B: the Na+-K+ pump moves Na+ in and K+ out of the fiber
options.C: extracellular K+ concentration is more than its intracellular concentration
options.D: if the resting membrane potential is moved to a less negative value, the fiber becomes more excitable

explanations.A: Incorrect. Intracellular K+ concentration is far higher than extracellular K+, so its concentration gradient favours K+ moving out of, not into, the fibre -- this option reverses the actual direction of the K+ gradient.
explanations.B: Incorrect. This reverses the Na+-K+ pump's actual direction: the pump moves Na+ out of and K+ into the cell (3 Na+ out for 2 K+ in), not Na+ in and K+ out as stated here.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Extracellular K+ concentration is much lower than intracellular K+ concentration, the opposite of what this option claims -- K+ is the dominant intracellular, not extracellular, cation.
explanations.D: Correct. The resting potential and threshold potential are both fixed reference points, and how close together they sit determines excitability. Moving the resting potential to a less negative value brings it closer to threshold, so a smaller additional depolarizing stimulus is needed to fire the fibre -- it becomes more excitable.

questions.subject: neuro
questions.learning_objective: State that shifting the resting membrane potential toward threshold (less negative) increases nerve fibre excitability.

questions.title: Extracellular calcium and excitability
questions.question: Excitability of the nerve fiber is increased in the following condition :

options.C: a decrease of Na+ concentration in ECF
options.D: a decrease in extracellular K+ concentration

explanations.A: Correct. Extracellular calcium normally stabilises voltage-gated Na+ channels, raising the threshold needed to open them. A fall in extracellular calcium (hypocalcaemia) removes some of that stabilisation, lowering the threshold and increasing excitability -- the mechanism behind hypocalcaemic tetany.
explanations.B: Incorrect. A rise in extracellular calcium increases the membrane-stabilising effect on Na+ channels, raising the threshold further and decreasing, not increasing, excitability -- the opposite direction from what this question asks about.
explanations.C: Incorrect. A decrease in extracellular Na+ concentration reduces the driving force for Na+ influx during depolarization, which would decrease the size of the action potential's rising phase, not increase excitability through the calcium-threshold mechanism this question tests.
explanations.D: Incorrect. A decrease in extracellular K+ concentration hyperpolarizes the membrane (moving it further from threshold), which decreases excitability, not increases it.

questions.subject: neuro
questions.learning_objective: State that a fall in extracellular calcium increases nerve fibre excitability (hypocalcaemic tetany).

questions.title: Mechanism of the absolute refractory period
questions.question: During absolute refractory period :

options.B: Na+ channels are inactivated by inner gates
options.C: stronger stimulus higher than threshold can excite the nerve fiber
options.D: coincides with whole duration of the action potential

explanations.A: Incorrect. Voltage-gated K+ channels do not have the same fast inactivation gate mechanism that Na+ channels do, and it is Na+ channel inactivation, not K+ channel inactivation, that defines the absolute refractory period.
explanations.B: Correct. Voltage-gated Na+ channels have a separate inactivation gate that closes shortly after the activation gate opens, regardless of continued depolarization. During the absolute refractory period, enough of these inactivation gates are already closed that a second stimulus, however strong, cannot force them open -- the channels needed for a second action potential are simply unavailable.
explanations.C: Incorrect. By definition, no stimulus of any strength -- however far above the normal threshold -- can excite the fibre during the absolute refractory period, because the Na+ channels required are inactivated, not merely harder to trigger.
explanations.D: Incorrect. The absolute refractory period spans roughly from the start of depolarization until repolarization is well underway, not the whole duration of the action potential -- the relative refractory period, during which excitability is reduced but not abolished, covers the remaining, later part.

questions.subject: neuro
questions.learning_objective: State that the absolute refractory period is caused by inactivation of voltage-gated Na+ channels' inner (inactivation) gates.
